speechtext:
am ready to admit that there are points in my hon. friend's resolution which require further study so that they can be harmonized with each other. But I point out that in the course of his remarks he expressed the hope that the

House would see fit to refer his resolution to a committee for study. In other words, he admitted there were points which ought to be studied further. I would also draw attention to a fact which should be known to all members of this chamber: the various senior citizens' and old age pensioners' organizations in Canada hold conventions from time to time at which they prepare briefs and submit requests to us. The items set out in this motion are the things for which they are asking, and even if some of them go a bit far, even if some of them do not harmonize with each other, I think it is perfectly proper that Parliament should be asked to give consideration to what they have suggested. Henee, in my opinion the proposal that this whole matter be referred to a special committee or to one of our standing committees is an appropriate one.
I was amused by the confidence which the new Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance displayed when he told us that one of these days we would be getting the white paper on social security. I hope that in his new position, even though he has held it for only a few days, he is privy to what goes on and knows whereof he speaks. I have to base my knowledge on what I hear out in the open, and out in the open I know that the question of doing something about social security has been in the Speech from the Throne presented to each of the sessions we have had since the election of this government. I know, also, that much work was put into what was known as the Willard report, or perhaps I should say the Willard reports. I know that for quite a while the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) said that consideration was being given to making those reports public. But we have never seen them and the time has been changed two or three times. Instead of getting to see the Willard report or reports, we were told about a year ago that there was to be a government white paper based on the work of Dr. Willard, the Deputy Minister of National Welfare.
When we were first told we would get a white paper, we were promised it would be down soon. Then we were told it would be down some time during the session and for a while this statement was made with the clear implication that we would get it before the House rose for the 1970 summer recess. Later this was modified and the Minister of National Health and Welfare told us we would get it before the House prorogued in October. We pinned him down repeatedly and he respond-
October 5, 1970

ed straightforwardly by telling the House we would have it before Parliament prorogued in October.
Well, we are now in October and know we shall prorogue the day after tomorrow. But when I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) during the oral question period this afternoon whether this particular commitment would be kept, he in effect said no; he told us there would be no white paper before the end of the present session. However, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance still thinks there will be a white paper, maybe next session or the one after that, or during the election campaign of 1972. I know that when I asked when we were likely to see this white paper, the Prime Minister did not tell me. Maybe it is so white it is blank; so white that there is nothing on it. The Prime Minister said, instead, that the matter might be mentioned in the Speech from the Throne on Thursday. Well, it was mentioned in the Speech from the Throne last year and the year before. I am not encouraged by these references and these promises. The fact of the matter is that nothing is being done.
Another thing I found amusing was the way in which the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance and the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) have stood up the principle of universality. My hon. friend from Surrey, who is a realist, tried to deal with the situation we find today, a hodge-podge of old age security arrangements, in an effort to get something done to help the old people now. The two hon. members who spoke after he sat down did not like that proposal because it would interfere with the pure principle of universality to which they say we were all committed back in 1952.
Mr. Speaker, I could take that line of argument a lot easier if I did not feel the hypocrisy behind it. It is the very government sitting over there which violated that principle by introducing the guaranteed income supplement and telling us we must move from universality to selectivity. Which way does my hon. friend the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance want it? He wants universality when my hon. friend from Surrey tries to do a little patch work, but when we ask for universality we are told that we have to go for selectivity. The net result is that nothing gets done. We have not seen the Willard Report. We have not seen the white paper within the time it was promised we would receive it. All we are given now is the chance to look at the Speech from the Throne
Old Age Security Pensions on Thursday morning. We will see what we get on Thursday, but I am afraid I have been around here long enough to know that if the election is to be in 1972 there is not going to be very much in a Speech from the Throne in 1970.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
This situation, Mr. Speaker, is a serious one. It is said that we are in the affluent age. All sorts of people are getting increases in wages, salaries, pensions and so on. We have done some of that around this place. We did it for the retired civil servants, retired members of the RCMP and retired armed forces personnel. Today a report by the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications was tabled. This is a good report. Indeed, it recommends that the same thing be done for retired employees of Canadian National Railways and calls upon other companies, both public and private, to follow suit. There are 800,000 old age pensioners in Canada today, senior citizens who have made their contribution to the life of this nation, who are so poor and so hard up that they qualify for the guaranteed income supplement. Indeed, there are 400,000 of them who qualify for the full amount, which really means they have virtually nothing at all. If this Parliament and the members in it care for our older people and have any heart at all, it is time to do something about them instead of just nitpicking at this resolution. What our pensioners need is an increase in their pensions to $150 a month, and they need it now.
I commend my hon. friend for bringing this subject before Parliament today and I regret there have not been any positive statements by the spokesmen for the Liberal party and the Conservative party.

subtopic: SHIPPING CONFERENCES EXEMPTION ACT

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of Bill C-184, to exempt certain shipping conference practices from the provisions of the Combines Investigations Act, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications, and motion No. 2 (Mr. Homer).

subtopic: SHIPPING CONFERENCES EXEMPTION ACT
subsubtopic: EXEMPTION OF CERTAIN PRACTICES FROM PROVISIONS OF COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the House went into private members' hour at five o'clock we were left with two cliff-hangers in this debate. The first related to how some 40 conferences could decide on identical rates between Canadian ports on the east coast to British ports and, second-and this is the cliff-hanger of particular interest to me and my area-why the rates from Halifax or Saint John to the United Kingdom should be the same as rates from points on the St. Lawrence east of Montreal, when we seem to have a 300-nauti-cal mile geographic advantage.
I related that attempts had been made, without success, to find out why this should be so when it flies in the face of all reason. I quoted evidence given by the former director of the Port of Halifax Commission. I turn now to remarks made by Mr. Craig S. Dickson, executive manager of the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission. He wrote the chairman of the Transport Committee on May 8 and I quote him in part as follows:
With reference to the proposed legislation set out in Bill C-184, this commission is in general agreement. It does wish, however, to draw to the committee's attention that there is one facet of the ocean shipping conference practices which works against the Maritime ports and exporters and importers of Atlantic Canada. This practice is the assessment of the same ocean rates to or from the
October 5, 1970

Maritime ports of Halifax, N.S., and Saint John, N.B., as from the inland ports of the St. Lawrence River, Montreal, P.Q., and east thereof. Despite the Maritime ports being geographically closer to most foreign countries than the St. Lawrence ports are, the rates of the ocean shipping conferences give no recognition of this fact.
Subsequently he stated:
The incongruity of this situation is emphasized when by section 16 of the National Transportation Act carriers subject to that act are required not to create through their actions prejudice to the public interest which goes "beyond any disadvantage that may be deemed to be inherent in ... location". At the same time Bill C-184 regularizes the practices of the shipping conferences including their practice of not recognizing the advantage inherent in the location of Maritime exporters and importers using Maritime ports.
On behalf of Maritime exporters and importers, this commission urges the members of this Standing Committee on Transport and Communications to take whatever steps are open to them individually and collectively to persuade the ocean shipping conferences to recognize the geographic advantage of Maritime ports in their ocean rates to and from these ports.
Such a step would be of material assistance to Maritime exporters in improving their export marketing position to the benefit not only of the Atlantic region but to Canada as a whole. Furthermore, the recommendations made herein do not require the expenditure of federal funds. In fact, by encouraging Maritime manufacturers to increase their participation in export markets through lower ocean rates from Maritime ports, there could be a lesser demand for expenditures under existing transportation programs in Atlantic Canada.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, he is not asking that any money be spent on the problem; he is just asking that a little common sense be exercised in dealing with the problem. As we get nowhere in unravelling this crazy mystery, may I quote a witness from the shipping conferences who appeared before the committee. He is W. J. McLaughlin, chairman of the Canada-United Kingdom Freight Conference. He told the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Homer):
We admit that the price is uniform and that we agree to the price. We do not deny that.
That statement is taken from the Minutes of Proceedings and Evidence of the committee No. 26, and he is referring to the uniformity of the rates as between St. Lawrence ports and Atlantic ports. The hon. member for Crowfoot asked:
In other words, you are saying that if one of your conference members lowered the rate to Halifax he would be breaking the conference rule after the

Mr. McLaughlin answered:
Basically when a company joins the conference it joins with the full knowledge that it joins a 22478-65i
Shipping Conferences Exemption Act rate-making group for this purpose because there is a wide segment of importers and exporters that demand and require the stability of rates. They prefer this stability of rates.
The hon. member for Crowfoot then said:
You fellows may get the idea that I am against you. I am not. I just admire the way you look after yourselves, because you are certainly not looking after the customers, nor is this bill.
I think my friend the hon. member for Crowfoot summed it up in a nutshell when he said those words. The bill ratifies and applies practices which surely are not in the interest of the Canadian user of shipping services. The other morning I had the horrendous experience of going to a freight handlers' hall in Halifax and seeing that 183 men out of 300 who had shown up for work that morning were disappointed because there was none.
For these reasons I support the amendment put forward by the hon. member for Crowfoot and I reject the philosophy of this bill. Perhaps the only thing that commends the bill to me is that its provisions are for three years and at the end of that period the shipping conferences will have to come here again. I hope at that time they will be able to say why this ridiculous practice is carried on. I hope they will then be able to answer the question that was asked several times that particular day and to which no reply was given.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to add a few comments to the discussion of this amendment to Bill C-184. I shall be very brief because I believe the minister wishes to make a few comments. Perhaps he wishes to close out the debate on the amendment. I really cannot see what a man with the perception and political skill of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson), with his political roots in the east, and having such competence would find objectionable in the amendment put forward by the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner). I will sit down right now if the minister is prepared to stand in his place and say he is prepared to accept the amendment.
Without going into the whole complicated area of shipping conference arrangements and practices as reviewed, diagnosed and defined in the Restrictive Trade Practices report which has already been referred to and tabled, I say very briefly there is no doubt that this is a cartel and that the Shipping Act is proposed to exempt certain of these companies from the Combines Investigation Act. Because cheap transportation is necessary to get Canadian goods to the world markets, I suppose this in part is a move ahead.
The point, however, is that in the east people often hear politicians especially say that the Atlantic and Nova Scotia form the wharf of the Atlantic and that we are in the middle of the deep blue because we are so close to European markets and the markets of Africa and other places. Yet in reality, because of the practices of these shipping conference companies there is no more advantage in being in Halifax than there is in being in Montreal, with all respect to Montreal. So we in the east feel somewhat aggrieved in that internally we have discrimination in respect of distance and externally, when we endeavour to sell our products in markets across the world, we do not have the advantage to which our geography has made us captive.
It is for that reason I cannot understand why the Minister of Transport, be he from any area, let alone one who has roots in the east, would be against an amendment that really does not go too far but, hopefully, would provide a little relief for those who would be greatly affected by the monopolistic and/or discriminatory rates which might be set up. I do not think there is any doubt about what this shipping conference does. I do not intend to read all of it, because the minister must have read part of it, but I want to repeat what the director said. I am refer-
October 5. 1970
ring to page 3 of the document headed "Shipping Conference Arrangements and Practices." He said, with no qualification, that these companies are parties to a combination in relation to commodities which may be the subject of trade or commerce and-leaving out certain things-that these combinations prevent and lessen competition.
Further on in the paragraph he says that these companies have conspired, combined, agreed or arranged to prevent or lessen unduly competition in the ocean transportation of those articles. The minister himself would be the first to agree that one of the objects, if not the main object, obviously is to set a rate and that one of the adverse effects of an agreement to set a rate is to lessen competition, so that we do not have the free flow on the market by which to define what it is right to have in a given circumstance.
As one who comes from the east I support this amendment which at least would start to shed some light and would, hopefully, make those who conspire to reduce or eliminate competition come before a government somewhere or the Canadian Transport Commission and explain their move. All that is necessary is to read-as the minister and other persons in his department have done-the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission's study of this problem. It reviews the practices in other countries. I shall not take the time of the House to review them tonight. However, the United States and Japan, two very large countries which have a large international trade, have taken government action to see that an international cartel or combination of cartels must file their agreements. In effect, they must substantiate them and if there is any discrimination there is a forum to which the natives of the country can apply for redress. As I understand it, the amendment of the hon. member for Crowfoot does not even begin to go that far, but at least it throws some light on this type of agreement and we would not have what seems to be the fundamental paradox as we struggle into the second half of the twentieth century, of the east having all the disadvantage of distance in our internal trade and having no geographical advantage in our external trade. This is a situation that I find very difficult to accept.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
I will close on this note. Agriculture was the subject of a little commotion in the House this afternoon, and quite rightly so because it was caused by a most important matter concerning Bill C-197, with which this House will
Shipping Conferences Exemption Act deal and which came into question this afternoon. I am referring to the feed freight policy. Some members of the cabinet do not believe there should be any such thing as a feed freight policy to haul feed grain across the country so that viable sections of Canada can develop our agricultural products. Fortunately that problem was diverted. We did not have to make a decision in the House last year on the matter, but there is a time limit on this problem which affects our internal trade. Here we are dealing with our external trade, and the east seems to be getting a raw deal. I hope the minister can explain the paradox that we have all the disadvantages, because of our position, in internal trade and none of the advantages that being the wharf of the Atlantic should give us.

Mr. Speaker, I did not anticipate that at this stage of the bill we would be in fact re-covering, as it were, many of the issues that were not only debated at length when the bill was first introduced but were dealt with at considerable length at the committee stage. I am not suggesting there is anything improper about the procedure and the discussion that has taken place tonight, but the fact is that we have been over this ground many times.
I do not want to take the time of the House to comment in detail on the references made by the last two speakers with regard to the apparent disparity that it is alleged exists between Halifax and Saint John, on the one hand, and the port of Montreal, for example, on the other. I can only say that I am somewhat surprised that someone representing the Montreal region has not seen fit to comment on this question. I am delighted to hear it, because the gentle weight of the criticism that has been aimed in my direction recently is that I have altogether favoured the east coast ports as opposed to Montreal. One has only to look at the wide range of comments coming these days from the shipping community and related interests in Montreal to appreciate that their point of view is not shared entirely by the three distinguished representatives from the Maritime provinces who have spoken tonight.
I do not believe it is possible to relate all the problems that are involved, in terms of the setting of rates, to the one issue that is before the House at the present time. The fact is that many of us, myself included, find it exceedingly difficult to understand fully how all forms of transportation arrive at the rate

8790	COMMONS
Shipping Conferences Exemption Act structures that they have. The examples that have been provided by hon. members from the Atlantic provinces have, of course, been repeated on earlier occasions by the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) in a different context when dealing with freight rates to the Prairie provinces, which do not indeed involve foreign shipping but are confined entirely to Canadian modes of transportation. At the same time they find that the rates, for example between Toronto, Montreal and Regina or Edmonton, are higher than if the same quantity and the same type of goods are shipped to Vancouver. These appear to the laymen to be obvious inconsistencies in the rate formulae which have been established by the various modes of transportation.
I can only say to the House that despite innumerable explorations by committees of the House and various other bodies, and despite a wide variety of royal commissions and studies of one nature or another, they have invariably come back to supporting the various forms of transportation in their ratesetting formulae. I think the National Transportation Act of 1967 made it clear that the competitive factors were to dominate, in terms of the establishment of various rates throughout Canada. Of course, if we are to remove some of what I regard as the inequities in some of the present rate structures, it appears that we will have to use mechanisms other than the National Transportation Act to do it.
However, may I point out with your indulgence, Mr. Speaker, that this is an aside and it is not germane to the matter now before the House. I mention it because, naturally, I share the questioning of members opposite as to why there is this differential in rates. But I do say-and I think they would be prepared to agree-that in recent times we have done a great deal to enhance what the hon. member for Annapolis Valley (Mr. Nowlan) has called the wharf of the Atlantic. I may say that it is now a much better wharf than it was even a few years ago, if one looks at the port of Halifax. Here I think we have to do a little horn-blowing, not as members of the government but indeed as a Parliament and as people from the area, and we have to admit that many tens of millions of dollars are being expended in the Atlantic provinces by the National Harbours Board and other agencies, including, for example, the province of Nova Scotia and Canadian National Railways. In Saint John, New Brunswick, a similar kind of expenditure is being undertaken.

DEBATES	October 5, 1970
So I repeat that we do have this inconsistency, which is a perfectly natural one when one considers the areas from which various members of this House come. For my part I am pleased to have had this endorsement, or indeed even criticism from Atlantic Canada, because I can now use it in rebuttal against those in other parts of the country who, quite contrary to what has been said this afternoon or this evening, have maintained that we are ignoring upper Canada in favour of what is undoubtedly the best part of the country. So much for that point.
I want to speak for a moment directly on the amendment of the hon. member for Crowfoot because I understand his position and I am not entirely in disagreement with the principles he is seeking to establish. But I suggest to him that there is a complication, and I think the hon. member will understand why it is not possible to support his amendment. He himself gave one reason for it, and at the same time indicated a certain inconsistency on the part of those who oppose sections of this bill, when he indicated this afternoon that the amendment moved by the hon. member for Regina Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) was in fact at odds with the one being proposed by the hon. member for Crowfoot, for a very simple reason.
The quandary I face is demonstrated obviously by both these gentlemen. One says, "Let the CTC have absolutely nothing to do with this." He says, "We want to take it out of their hands completely. On the other hand, the hon. member for Crowfoot says, "We will not only keep the CTC in the picture but we want to enhance their responsibility far more than even the government is prepared to do." It is clear that we cannot meet both points of view, and in fact the truth of the matter is that neither point of view is on all fours with the basic objectives of this bill. The hon. member for Crowfoot has made clear what he wishes to have done. His amendment reads:
For the purposes of this act, a tariff, patronage contract, arrangement, agreement or contract shall not be valid unless and until approved by an order of the commission as just and reasonable and in the public interest-
Here I would like to draw his attention to the following words:
-as defined in section 16 of the National Transportation Act-
The definition of "public interest" in section 16 (1) (b) of the National Transportation Act reads as follows:
the expression "public interest" includes, without limiting the generality thereof, the public interest as described in section 1.

If I can now take hon. members through the bill still further, section 1 of the National Transportation Act is a declaration of the national transportation policy, and that policy rejects, within limits, rate approval as a means of regulation. Therefore, the effect of the proposed amendment would be to reverse this aspect of the national transportation policy and so, in effect, frustrate the law. From long experience I have known that the last thing my hon. friend from Crowfoot would wish to do would be to frustrate the law, even in a small way.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
Bill C-184 deals with shipping conferences which, as 1 would like to call to the attention of hon. members, serve Canada's overseas foreign trade. Obviously, in every instance where it is foreign trade of which we are speaking there is at least one other country involved. A statute which, in these circumstances, requires a formal finding of public interest in the various matters cited in the proposed amendment could, because of opposing views at the other end of the route, over which we do not have control, result in grave and unnecessary international difficulties and become an impediment to trade.
I would point out that even the hon. member for Halifax, who made some very sound observations, in the quotations he put forward indicated that some of the chief spokesmen for Maritime Canada had shown they were in agreement with the basic objectives of the bill. I suggest that anyone who has experience with shipping will recognize it is quite impossible, when dealing internationally, to have unilateral power in the hands of an organization such as the CTC, or even the restrictive trade practices agency, to deal with such a matter in the way proposed by the amendment. These matters were thought through very carefully. As I have said from the very first moment I made reference to this measure in the House, I do what I am doing here with a measure of reluctance because this is not the kind of measure that is totally protective of

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am afraid I cannot match the oratory of my friend the hon. member for Edmonton Centre (Mr. Paproski). I confess I do not feel inclined to try to do so when one realizes that not only has the Hudson's Bay Company played a part in developing this country but has done a fair amount of skinning of our people, both in the past and in the present. Having said that, however, I think I shall confine myself to recognizing that there is a certain historicity about what we are doing. We are in fact agreeing to the transfer of the head office of the company not only from England to Canada but from London to Winnipeg, and not only to Winnipeg but to the heart of Winnipeg North Centre. So I am very happy to indicate our support of this bill.
I suppose one reason we do not take off into flights of oratory is that we realize that merely to transfer the head office is not everything. There is the whole question of ownership and who makes the profit out of an organization such as this. Hon. members who have been following the news of the last weekend would not be surprised if I were to make a speech about the whole question of foreign ownership and the desirability of certain other head offices being transferred to Canada. Mr. Speaker, I am sure Your Honour and all members of the House have been moved by the eloquence of the hon. member for Edmonton Centre (Mr. Paproski) in the historical narration he gave of the activities of the Hudson's Bay Company. I am sure we are appreciative of his eloquence on this occasion. I am sure, also, that the reference by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) to skinning had reference to the activities of the company
Establishment of Canadian Corporation as the largest fur trading company in the world.
For the sake of the record I simply wish to outline some of the corporate details of the bill in order to explain briefly what it is intended to do, simply because I will be moving at the appropriate time that there be unanimous consent to deal with the bill in Committee of the Whole this evening. Now that 95 per cent of the assets of the company and 98 per cent of its employees are located in Canada, the company on attaining its 300th birth date has expressed the wish to become a "Canadian company". This calls for a transfer of jurisdiction which is an unusual procedure and, as a matter of fact, we know of almost no precedent. Because the company operated under a royal charter granted some 300 years ago, it was necessary to devise a procedure to cover the present instance. The Privy Council of the United Kingdom, by supplementary letters patent issued on May 29, 1970, revoked all amendments to and all sections of the original charter of 300 years ago except the original incorporating section. These supplementary letters patent permit the company to continue under the authority of the government of Canada. On the same day last spring the Canadian Privy Council issued letters patent under the Great Seal of Canada under the original royal charter.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
The effect of that procedure is to continue the English corporate entity into a Canadian one. In Canada our commercial corporations are being administered under a general act of parliament, the Canada Corporations Act. Opportunity was taken at that time in the spring to change the shares of the company from one English pound par value to no par value shares. A number of restrictions are imposed by the letters patent on the transfer of shares. These are provided for in the bill. This has reference to what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre had to say. Not more than 25 per cent of the shares may be held by non-residents of Canada or the United Kingdom. For a five-year transitional period from May 29, 1970, not more than 10 per cent of the shares may be held by any one person or associated group of persons.
I should mention in passing, Mr. Speaker, that 10 per cent of the outstanding shares are presently held in Canada, 86 per cent in the United Kingdom and 4 per cent in other parts of the world. The purpose of introducing the bill before the House is to bring the company incorporated under special letters patent

Establishment of Canadian Corporation granted by Canada under the Canada Corporations Act. As hon. members see, the bill is rather short because very few exemptions from the Canada Corporations Act have been requested by the company.
I ask for the unanimous consent of the House to move into Committee of the Whole and deal with the bill this evening, if it is the will of the House to do so. I thank hon. members for agreeing to deal with this somewhat technical corporate matter at this late day in this session, and I hope we can dispose of it this evening.
